## Question 1:

### Recreate the following image with the [housing data](https://github.com/byuidatascience/data4dwellings/raw/master/data-raw/dwellings_denver/dwellings_denver.csv):

```{python}
# Question 1 Code

url_housing = "https://github.com/byuidatascience/data4dwellings/raw/master/data-raw/dwellings_denver/dwellings_denver.csv"
denver = pd.read_csv(url_housing)

# Keep only the three "standard" house types shown in the chart legend
house_types = ['ONE-STORY', 'SPLIT LEVEL', 'TWO-STORY']
denver_sub = denver[denver['arcstyle'].isin(house_types)]

color_map = {
    'ONE-STORY': '#2CA88E',
    'SPLIT LEVEL': '#E58429',
    'TWO-STORY': '#9C88C4'
}

fig = px.scatter(
    denver_sub,
    x='yrbuilt',
    y='livearea',
    color='arcstyle',
    color_discrete_map=color_map,
    log_y=True,
    title="Thank goodness the 21st century doesn't have split levels",
    labels={
        'yrbuilt': 'Year home was built',
        'livearea': 'Square footage of home (log)',
        'arcstyle': 'Standard house types'
    }
)
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=6, opacity=0.7))
fig.update_layout(
    legend_title_text='Standard house types',
    legend=dict(orientation='h', yanchor='top', y=-0.2, xanchor='center', x=0.5)
)
fig.show()
```

## Question 2:

### Fix the series to all be `np.nan` and calculate the standard deviation (2 decimal places):

```{python}
# Question 2 Code

problem = pd.Series(['N/A', 15, 22, 45, 31, -999, 21, 2, 0, 0, 0, 'broken'])

# Convert to numeric, turning non-numeric strings ('N/A', 'broken') into NaN
problem = pd.to_numeric(problem, errors='coerce')

# -999 is a valid number as far as pd.to_numeric is concerned, so it has to be
# replaced separately since it's a sentinel/placeholder value, not real data
problem = problem.replace(-999, np.nan)

std_dev = round(problem.std(), 2)
std_dev
```

## Question 3:

### Split the `age` category into two columns and use the `minimum age` and re-create this histogram:

```{python}
# Question 3 Code

people = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ['Joseph', 'Maria', 'Edmond', 'Fay', 'Rachel', 'George', 'Hector',
             'Wesley', 'Silas', 'Leslie', 'Janet', 'Norman'],
    "age": ["10-19", "10-19", "20-29", "50-59", "10-19", "40-49",
            "50-59", "30-39", "60-69", "50-59", "10-19", "20-29"]
})

# Split "age" into min_age and max_age columns
people[['min_age', 'max_age']] = people['age'].str.split('-', expand=True).astype(int)

fig = px.histogram(
    people,
    x='min_age',
    title='Count of People by Minimum Age',
    labels={'min_age': 'Minimum Age'}
)
fig.update_traces(xbins=dict(start=0, end=70, size=10))
fig.update_layout(bargap=0.1)
fig.show()
```

## Question 4:

### Use the [cleaned Star Wars data](http://byuistats.github.io/CSE250-Course/data/clean_starwars.csv) to predict the gender of the respondent to the survey. Report your accuracy and a feature importance plot with the top 10 most important features:

* Use `test_size = .20` and `random_state = 2020` in `train_test_split()`
* Use the `GradientBoostingClassifier()` method.

```{python}
# Question 4 Code

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

url_sw = "http://byuistats.github.io/CSE250-Course/data/clean_starwars.csv"
sw = pd.read_csv(url_sw)

# Drop rows with a missing target
sw = sw.dropna(subset=['gender'])

X = sw.drop(columns=['gender'])
y = sw['gender']

# Fill any remaining missing feature values (the dataset is already dummy-encoded)
X = X.fillna(0)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=.20, random_state=2020
)

model = GradientBoostingClassifier()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy:.4f}")

# Top 10 feature importances
importances = pd.Series(model.feature_importances_, index=X.columns)
top10 = importances.sort_values(ascending=False).head(10).sort_values()

fig = px.bar(
    top10,
    x=top10.values,
    y=top10.index,
    orientation='h',
    title='Top 10 Most Important Features for Predicting Gender',
    labels={'x': 'Feature Importance', 'y': 'Feature'}
)
fig.show()
```
